description: We are a team of five technology professionals with diverse expertise in software development and AI integration. Together, we're building an health-monitoring platform for astronauts that tracks vital signs, detects potential health risks, and provides real-time health insights to support early intervention and safer space missions.
summary: AstroMed is a NASA Space Apps prototype for long-duration deep-space flight (MTV-1 Mars transit, ~20-minute Earth delay). It gives each astronaut a personal console to assess and improve health without waiting on Earth: guided daily checks (blood pressure, glucose, temperature, mood, sleep, hydration), wearable vitals with live ECG and HRV trends, habitat limits for CO₂ and radiation, exercise and sleep logging, a reaction-time cognitive test, injury and cycle tracking, and a clickable body map linked to NASA’s five spaceflight hazards (RIDGE). Results use green/amber/red status, monitoring rules, and plain-language next steps; when the link is down, an on-device AI co-pilot still triages using crew baselines and ISS-style protocols, while vitals and logs queue offline and sync later. Mission structure supports super admin onboarding, per-crew access, commander overviews, and oversight dashboards that surface alerts and co-pilot history for flight surgeons. Health missions, streaks, patches, and a Space Cat companion encourage daily habits. Thresholds draw on NASA HRP evidence and open Inspiration4 OSDR crew labs. Hackathon prototype—not official NASA or medical advice.
details:
AstroMed — Astronaut Health Monitoring Console

Getting someone to Mars and keeping that person safe and healthy throughout the journey are two different challenges. Twenty light-minutes from Earth, there is no ground flight surgeon on instant call. AstroMed is a research and educational prototype that helps astronauts monitor personal health changes, interpret physiological trends, and follow traceable mission guidance when real-time medical support from Earth is unavailable.

Designed around NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight, AstroMed delivers five-hazard health support with traceable rules and offline continuity—uniting daily self-check telemetry, personal pre-flight baseline comparisons (modeled with de-identified SpaceX Inspiration4 crew laboratory data from NASA OSDR), an interactive 3D anatomical Body Map, live space-weather context, an in-browser quantized AI co-pilot, and role-enforced oversight (/oversight) for commanders and flight surgeons. AstroMed supports crew self-awareness and structured follow-up documentation; it does not diagnose disease or eliminate the hazards of spaceflight.

What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

1. Daily Self-Check & Clinical Telemetry: Crew members complete a guided daily self-check covering blood pressure, fasting/non-fasting blood sugar, body temperature, subjective mood, sleep duration, and hydration, alongside live clinical telemetry (heart rate, SpO2, heart rate variability, ECG waveform view, and radiation exposure).

2. Personal Baseline & Mission Threshold Evaluation: Incoming readings are evaluated against configurable mission thresholds and each crew member’s own pre-flight baseline, demonstrated using de-identified SpaceX Inspiration4 laboratory profiles from NASA OSDR (OSD-569 and OSD-575).

3. Interactive 3D Body Map & RIDGE Hazard Filtering: Astronauts inspect organ systems (Eyes, Lungs, Heart, Blood & Immune, Brain & Mind, Reproductive, Bones & Muscles) on a rotatable 3D scan, filter by NASA’s five RIDGE hazards, and review plain-language explanations and medical-kit countermeasures.

4. My Monitoring, Habitat Routine & Cognitive Alertness: Time-series sparklines (7-, 14-, and 30-day windows) track longitudinal trends and raise Green (Nominal), Amber (Caution), or Red (Warning) alerts with expandable 'Why this alerted' rationale. Habitat & Routine tracks cabin ppCO2, dose rate, live NOAA space weather, exercise adherence (ARED, T2, CEVIS), and a 3-minute Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT).

5. On-Device Flight Surgeon Co-Pilot & Offline Sync Queue: During link delays (simulated at 20m 04s) or communication blackouts, astronauts consult a local quantized LLAMA-3.2-1B-Q4 co-pilot running directly in the browser (with a deterministic rules-based fallback) while vitals, logs, and transcripts queue locally in IndexedDB until Earth synchronization resumes.

6. Role-Based Mission Oversight (/oversight & /admin): Server-enforced access control ensures standard crew logins (e.g., John, EV1) view only their own records; Mission Commander Vance views all of MTV-1; Flight Surgeon Dr. Amara Lewis (/oversight) reviews assigned crews’ vitals, alerts (with acknowledge/resolve notes), and full co-pilot transcripts; Ground Control views all missions; and Super Admin (/admin) configures mission groups, alert rules, and audit logs.


Figure 1: Interactive 3D Body Map & RIDGE Hazard Filter — Clicking Heart reveals a WARNING flag driven by a -14% drop in lab potassium (3.00 mmol/L vs. own pre-flight baseline from NASA OSDR OSD-569/OSD-575), paired with physiological explanations, medical-kit guidance, and the on-device LLAMA-3.2-1B-Q4 Flight Surgeon Co-Pilot.

1.2 Coverage Across NASA’s Five Human Spaceflight Hazards

Each module in AstroMed maps directly to one or more of NASA’s five human spaceflight hazards (RIDGE), pairing concrete software mechanisms with transparent prototype boundaries:

  • Space Radiation
    • Operational Challenge: Elevated Galactic Cosmic Radiation (GCR) and acute solar particle events.
    • AstroMed Mechanism: Integrates live NOAA SWPC feeds (S0/R0/G0 scales, >=10 MeV proton flux, X-ray flux, Kp index) alongside cabin dose-rate telemetry (0.074 mSv/hr vs. SHELTER 1.0).
    • Prototype Scope & Limitation: External space-weather feeds provide environmental context, not personal dosimetry.
    • Operational Challenge: Behavioral fatigue, sleep disruption, and circadian drift on long transits.
    • AstroMed Mechanism: Tracks sleep duration (6h 36m vs. 8.5 h target), daily mood (3/5), and 3-minute PVT alertness, paired with an interactive Space Cat morale companion.
    • Prototype Scope & Limitation: Supports behavioral routine adherence; not a psychiatric diagnostic or clinical treatment tool.
    • Operational Challenge: Cardiovascular deconditioning, cephalad fluid shifts, and bone/muscle loss.
    • AstroMed Mechanism: Monitors exercise adherence across Resistance (ARED), Treadmill (T2), and Cycle (CEVIS) (104/150 min, 69%) and maps organ-specific gravity impacts on the 3D Body Map.
    • Prototype Scope & Limitation: Tracks activity adherence and physiological trends; software alone cannot measure bone density.
    • Operational Challenge: Cabin CO2 accumulation and closed-loop life-support fluctuations.
    • AstroMed Mechanism: Displays Module 3 ppCO2 (2.4 mmHg vs. FLIGHT RULE 4.0) with visual threshold bars and procedural shielding / air-scrubber boost prompts.
    • Prototype Scope & Limitation: Displays environmental context and procedural prompts rather than directly actuating spacecraft hardware.
    • Operational Challenge: One-way communication latency (20m 04s) and deep-space link blackouts.
    • AstroMed Mechanism: Executes offline-first local storage (Dexie), an in-browser LLAMA-3.2-1B-Q4 co-pilot, and a queued Earth sync log (44 records waiting).
    • Prototype Scope & Limitation: Live NOAA and NASA DONKI external feeds require an active network connection to refresh.

Figure 2: Habitat & Routine Dashboard — Displaying Module 3 ppCO2 (2.4 mmHg), cabin radiation dose rate (0.074 mSv/hr), live NOAA SWPC solar telemetry (Quiet Sun, S0/R0/G0), and ARED/T2/CEVIS exercise and sleep adherence.



1.3 Reproducible Prototype Walkthrough (Verifiable Case Study)

Reproducible Walkthrough: Multi-System Baseline & Threshold Evaluation (EV1 John • MET 304/06:41:13)

•  Data Provenance Label: De-identified historical SpaceX Inspiration4 laboratory sample mapped from NASA OSDR OSD-569 & OSD-575 (subjects C001–C004) combined with simulated Mars-transit vitals for crew profile John (EV1-Crew).

•  Inputs & Units: Lab potassium 3.00 mmol/L, lab sodium 137 mmol/L, heart rate 75 bpm (normal sinus rhythm, HRV 63 ms), self-check BP 100/80 mmHg, SpO2 98%, body temperature 32.0 °C, and daily sleep 5.0 h.

•  Configured Rules & Baselines: Potassium is -14% below the crew member's own pre-flight baseline and below clinical reference limits; body temperature is below the 35.0 °C red threshold; sleep is below the 7.0 h amber threshold.

•  Observed Interface Output: On the 3D Body Map (Figure 2), Heart flags WARNING while Lungs remain NOMINAL and Eyes, Brain & mind, Blood & immune, Reproductive, and Bones & muscles show CAUTION. Selecting Heart explains how hypokalemia and microgravity fluid shifts affect cardiac rhythm and recommends taking a potassium supplement from the medical kit, eating potassium-rich food, and rechecking in 24 h (citing OSD-569 · OSD-575).

•  Follow-Up & Limitations: In My Monitoring (Figure 4), the astronaut inspects 'Why this alerted', acknowledges both active alerts with notes, and queues 44 records for Earth sync. Because Inspiration4 reflects a 3-day Low Earth Orbit mission, it serves as an educational baseline demonstration rather than real-time deep-space clinical diagnostics.

2.  What Benefits Does It Have?

Key Operational & Human-Factors Benefits

•  Immediate Visual Clarity: Color-coded status badges (NOMINAL, CAUTION, WARNING), 7/14/30-day sparklines with dashed amber/red threshold lines, and an interactive 3D Body Map let astronauts assess multi-system status in seconds.

•  Traceable, Evidence-Linked Guidance: Every alert exposes 'Why this alerted' and 'Explain this alert' drawers tied directly to personal-baseline deltas, mission rules, and NASA HRP / OSDR source rationale rather than opaque black-box scores.

•  Resilience During Disconnection: Local IndexedDB storage (Dexie) and on-device WebLLM inference (LLAMA-3.2-1B-Q4) ensure astronauts can log vitals, review countermeasures, and ask protocol questions even during complete Earth link blackouts.

•  Non-Punitive Habit Reinforcement: Daily health missions and achievement patches explicitly reward consistent self-care habits (check-ins, exercise, sleep, PVT alertness) rather than raw biometric scores—ensuring crew members are never penalized for reporting illness.

•  Accountable Oversight (/oversight): Flight surgeons and mission commanders review longitudinal trends, acknowledge or resolve alerts with clinical notes, and inspect full co-pilot transcripts once telemetry syncs, without compromising crew role boundaries.


Figure 3: My Monitoring — Active threshold alerts with crew acknowledgement notes and 14-day longitudinal sparklines.

3.  What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?

•  Near-Term Deep-Space Mission Readiness: Equips astronauts on extended lunar, orbital, and Mars-transit missions to recognize subtle physiological deviations early, sustain daily preventive routines (exercise, sleep hygiene, hydration, cognitive alertness), and maintain structured, auditable health logs across multi-minute communication delays.

•  Bridging Crew Autonomy and Ground Flight Surgeons: Rather than replacing ground medical teams, AstroMed improves the signal-to-noise ratio of asynchronous telemetry—delivering trends, acknowledged alerts, crew field notes, and full on-device co-pilot transcripts to /oversight as soon as a downlink window opens.

•  Future Terrestrial Adaptation & Spin-Off Potential: Beyond spaceflight, AstroMed’s offline-first sync architecture, personal-baseline tracking, and local browser AI assistant can be adapted—following appropriate regulatory validation, clinical governance, and localized protocols—for remote rural clinics, maritime vessels, polar research bases, and off-grid humanitarian deployments.


4.  Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

AstroMed is built as a modern, offline-capable full-stack web application designed to run in any standard desktop or tablet browser, leveraging WebGPU hardware acceleration when available for local LLM inference:

Frontend & 3D UI

•  Technologies, Languages & Sources: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Three.js

•  Role in AstroMed Architecture: Responsive mission console, time-series sparklines, RIDGE hazard strip, interactive 3D anatomical Body Map, and 3D Space Cat companion.

Backend, Database & Cloud

•  Technologies, Languages & Sources: PostgreSQL, Prisma ORM, Neon, Vercel

•  Role in AstroMed Architecture: Relational schema for crew profiles, vitals, alerts, audit logs, and mission groups; server-enforced RBAC across crew, /oversight, and /admin.

Offline-First & Edge AI

•  Technologies, Languages & Sources: Dexie (IndexedDB), WebLLM (LLAMA-3.2-1B-Q4), WebGPU, Web Speech API

•  Role in AstroMed Architecture: Client-side offline storage and sync queue; local quantized Llama 3.2 1B Flight Surgeon Co-Pilot with deterministic rules-based fallback; optional online voice check-in.

Testing & QA

•  Technologies, Languages & Sources: Vitest, Playwright

•  Role in AstroMed Architecture: Automated unit tests for threshold rules and baseline calculations; end-to-end browser tests for offline queuing, sync, and role access.

NASA OSDR & HRP Sources

•  Technologies, Languages & Sources: NASA OSDR (OSD-569, OSD-575, OSD-195), NASA HRP Five Hazards / RIDGE, NASA-STD-3001

•  Role in AstroMed Architecture: De-identified Inspiration4 pre-flight vs. post-flight whole-blood CBC (OSD-569) and serum metabolic/cytokine (OSD-575) baseline examples; bedrest muscle evidence (OSD-195); human-system standards.

Space Weather Feeds

•  Technologies, Languages & Sources: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) & NASA DONKI API

•  Role in AstroMed Architecture: Real-time S/R/G space-weather scales, >=10 MeV proton flux, X-ray flux, Kp index, and solar event alerts with graceful unavailable-feed fallback.

AI Use & Team Contribution Statement: Our team used AI tools during development for coding assistance, brainstorming, deeper literature review, and NASA OSDR dataset discovery. All scientific source selection, problem framing, clinical boundary decisions, rule thresholds, and system architecture were authored and verified by our team. We explicitly distinguish development-time AI assistance from the local, quantized LLAMA-3.2-1B-Q4 Flight Surgeon Co-Pilot embedded inside the AstroMed prototype.

5.  How Is Your Project Creative?

•  Hazard-to-Organ 3D Interactive Body Map (RIDGE + Three.js): Rather than presenting isolated tables of lab values, AstroMed lets astronauts toggle NASA’s five hazards (R, I, D, G, E) on a rotatable 3D human scan to immediately visualize which organs are affected, compare pre-flight vs. in-flight biomarkers, and retrieve actionable medical-kit steps in one unified view.

•  Morale-Centered Gamification (Space Cat & Non-Punitive Habit Patches): To counter long-duration isolation without gamifying illness, astronauts earn points by completing healthy routines (daily self-check, exercise, sleep, 3-minute PVT reaction test) to unlock mission patches (First light, Ignition, Orbit, Transit, Bone guardian) and feed an interactive 3D Space Cat companion whose voice mimicry stays strictly local to the browser tab.

•  Authentic Deep-Space Operational Realism: The interface simulates Mission Elapsed Time (MET), a 20m 04s Earth link delay, explicit offline queue states, and transparent status notices distinguishing offline on-device AI capabilities from network-dependent browser voice typing.

Figure 5A: Today’s Health Missions & Patches — Rewarding self-care habits, never raw biometric scores.

Figure 5B: Space Cat Companion — Morale support fueled by health-mission points with local-only voice echo.

6.  What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

•  Personal Pre-Flight Baselines vs. Population Norms: Microgravity alters baseline fluid distribution, blood counts, and metabolic markers. AstroMed evaluates percentage deltas relative to each astronaut’s own pre-flight baseline (modeled via Inspiration4 L-92/L-44/L-3 vs. post-flight samples) alongside standard clinical reference intervals.

•  Strict Clinical Boundaries & Non-Diagnostic Integrity: To prevent over-reliance on automated alerts, every screen and alert drawer frames outputs as research-informed self-monitoring guidance—never autonomous medical diagnosis—and requires human acknowledgement and follow-up notes.

•  Data Provenance Transparency & Graceful Degradation: The UI explicitly labels historical Inspiration4 research samples, demo profiles, and live NOAA space-weather feeds. Missing daily entries render cleanly as dashed intervals on 14-day sparklines, external API outages (such as DONKI) degrade gracefully without blocking workflows, and devices without WebGPU seamlessly fall back to deterministic rule guidance.

•  Multi-Role Privacy & Server-Enforced Access Control: Crew medical privacy and operational command require strict separation of duties. Server-side authorization isolates individual crew consoles (John, Cho, Silva), commander group views (CDR Vance), assigned flight-surgeon oversight (/oversight, Dr. Amara Lewis), ground control, and system administration (/admin).

•  Engineering Validation & Testing Roadmap: Our Vitest and Playwright verification suite tests offline IndexedDB persistence across page reloads, sync-queue reconciliation upon reconnection, duplicate-record prevention, threshold-boundary transitions, and server-enforced RBAC isolation, while clearly separating software verification from future clinical validation.

Appendix.  Judge Access, Demo Credentials & 12-Minute Guided Tour

Judges can explore the live prototype immediately at https://astro-med-ashy.vercel.app or jump directly to the flight-surgeon portal at https://astro-med-ashy.vercel.app/oversight using the demo accounts below (universal demo password: password):

Astronaut — John (EV1)

•  Email Login: john@aahms.demo

•  Route & Access Scope: / (Personal Console Only)

•  Suggested Judge Verification Step: Inspect My Vitals & ECG; log BP 118/102 in Daily Check to trigger a Red alert; explore Body Map (Heart WARNING) & ask Co-Pilot.

Flight Surgeon — Dr. Amara Lewis

•  Email Login: surgeon@aahms.demo

•  Route & Access Scope: /oversight (Assigned MTV-1)

•  Suggested Judge Verification Step: Review John's synced health logs, read full AI Co-Pilot transcripts from Part 1, and acknowledge or resolve active alerts with notes.

Mission Commander — Vance (CDR)

•  Email Login: vance@aahms.demo

•  Route & Access Scope: / (All MTV-1 Crew)

•  Suggested Judge Verification Step: Switch across MTV-1 crew members (John, Vance, Cho, Silva) to verify commander-level group readiness visibility.

Ground Control

•  Email Login: ground@aahms.demo

•  Route & Access Scope: /oversight (All Missions)

•  Suggested Judge Verification Step: Confirm cross-mission visibility across both MTV-1 and MTV-2 crews.

Super Admin

•  Email Login: admin@aahms.demo

•  Route & Access Scope: /admin (System Governance)

•  Suggested Judge Verification Step: Manage mission group assignments, tune alert rule thresholds, and inspect the immutable system audit log.
